01.note: Rav Dimi, the brother of Rav Safra, fell ill, and Rav Safra came to visit him. Rav Dimi told those present that blessing was coming to him, because he had kept every teaching of the Sages. Rav Safra asked whether he had kept the teaching that a person should never speak about another's goodness in front of others, since praise leads to talk of his faults. Rav Dimi answered that he had never heard that teaching, but had he heard it, he would have kept it.
01.why: The Gemara has just quoted this warning against praising people in public as Rav Dimi's own teaching. This alternative version says it was not his: it came up in this conversation, where he admitted he had never heard it.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: Rav Safra's brother; while ill, he claims to have kept every teaching of the Sages.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Rav Dimi's brother, who visits him and asks about the teaching on praising others.

02.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri calls heaven and earth as his witnesses: many times he complained about Akiva to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and Akiva was lashed, that is, punished, because of him. Yet each time Akiva only loved him more. His experience bears out the verse in Proverbs: do not rebuke a scorner lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man and he will love you.
02.why: Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaria have just doubted that anyone in their generation can accept rebuke, or give it properly. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri's testimony offers Akiva as a man who took rebuke again and again and loved the one who gave it.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri
people.about: Testifies that he often complained about Akiva to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

people.name: Akiva
people.about: Was punished many times because of Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri's complaints, and loved him all the more.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The authority before whom Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri brought his complaints about Akiva.

03.note: Rav Huna and Ḥiyya bar Rav were sitting before Shmuel when Ḥiyya bar Rav complained: See, Master, Rav Huna is causing me distress. Rav Huna took it upon himself not to do so again. Once Ḥiyya bar Rav had left, Rav Huna told Shmuel what Ḥiyya had done to him. Shmuel asked why he had not said this to Ḥiyya's face, and Rav Huna answered: Heaven forbid that the son of Rav should be humiliated because of me.
03.why: Rabbi Shimon has just told his son that humility, even when not for its own sake, outranks rebuke for its own sake. The Gemara asks what each looks like, and this incident shows both: Rav Huna's earlier private rebuke, and his yielding only to spare Rav's son shame.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Accused of distressing Ḥiyya bar Rav; he backs down rather than shame him in public.

people.name: Ḥiyya bar Rav
people.about: Rav's son, who complains to Shmuel that Rav Huna is distressing him.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The teacher before whom both men were sitting.

04.note: The mother of Yirmatya vowed to give the Temple the weight of her daughter. She went up to Jerusalem, had her daughter weighed, and gave her weight in gold.
04.why: The mishna rules that a vow of one's weight is paid in silver or gold as specified. The Gemara asks whether this incident, where gold was paid without specifying, contradicts that, and answers that a distinguished person pays according to status; she was very wealthy.

people.name: the mother of Yirmatya
people.about: A very wealthy woman, the Gemara says, who vowed her daughter's weight to the Temple.

terms.meaning: The core collection of early rabbinic teachings; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.
The fund that received money and goods vowed to the Temple in Jerusalem.

04.flag: The STORY segments (4-10) hold only one narrative sentence, the mother of Yirmatya's vow (stated in 4 and repeated in 10); segments 5-8 are unrelated legal rulings on vowing a forearm's weight and on paying in pitch or onions.

05.note: Moshe bar Atzrei had guaranteed his daughter-in-law's marriage contract, and his son Rav Huna, a Torah scholar, was hard-pressed for money. Abaye asked whether no one would advise Rav Huna to divorce his wife, let her collect her marriage contract from his father the guarantor, and then remarry her. Rava objected that the mishna requires such a husband to vow to have no benefit from her; the Gemara explains that Abaye would have him divorce outside the court. In the end it emerged that Rav Huna was a priest, so he could not have remarried her, and Abaye said: poverty follows the poor.
05.why: The mishna, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, makes a divorcing husband vow off benefit from his wife when a guarantor backs her marriage contract, lest the couple collude. Abaye's plan is that very collusion, and the Gemara then asks how Abaye could propose it.

people.name: Moshe bar Atzrei
people.about: Guarantor of his daughter-in-law's marriage contract; Rav Huna's father.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Moshe bar Atzrei's son, a Torah scholar short of money, who turns out to be a priest.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Proposes the divorce-and-remarry plan, then sums up the outcome with a saying about poverty.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Objects to Abaye's plan on the basis of the mishna.

terms.meaning: A husband's written commitment to pay his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies. A guarantor can promise to pay it if the husband does not.
A descendant of Aaron. Torah law forbids a priest to marry a divorced woman, even his own former wife.

06.note: A certain man wanted to give away more than a fifth of his property to charity, and his friend would not let him. One version says the friend was Rabbi Yeshevav. Another says Rabbi Yeshevav was the one who wanted to give too much, and the friend who stopped him was Rabbi Akiva.
06.why: The Gemara has just cited Rabbi Ila's report that the Sages at Usha ruled that no one should give more than a fifth of his money to charity, the view it ties to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya. This incident shows that limit being enforced.

people.name: Rabbi Yeshevav
people.about: In one version, the friend who stopped a man from giving too much charity; in the other, the man who was stopped.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: In the second version, the friend who stopped Rabbi Yeshevav.

07.note: Rabbi Yehuda reported that Baitos ben Zunin made a conditional sale of his field under the direction of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and that the buyer ate the field's produce. The Rabbis answered that this proves nothing: in that case it was the seller who ate the produce, not the buyer.
07.why: A baraita forbids a lender holding a field by conditional sale to eat its produce, since if the loan is repaid that would be interest; Rabbi Yehuda permits it and cites this case. Rabbi Yoḥanan uses the dispute to explain why the mishna calls a walled-city house redemption only like interest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Cites the case to support his view that the buyer may eat the produce.

people.name: Baitos ben Zunin
people.about: Made a conditional sale of his field.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Directed how Baitos ben Zunin's sale was arranged.

terms.meaning: A borrower sells his field to the lender on condition that the sale takes effect only if the loan is not repaid on time; if it is repaid, the sale is cancelled.

08.note: Mar Zutra visited Rav Ashi's home, and they offered him food. They set meat before him, saying: Eat, Master, it is especially healthful, because it is a firstborn. He asked where it came from, and they said a certain priest had sold it to them. Mar Zutra asked whether they did not hold, with Rav Huna son of Rabbi Yehoshua, that this looks like a priest helping at the threshing floor; they said no, since they had bought it. He pressed them with a mishna that forbids handing a firstborn to a priest early for the same reason. They replied that there the favor is plain to see, while here they had simply bought it.
08.why: Rav Huna son of Rabbi Yehoshua has just explained that a priest may not sell an unblemished firstborn to an Israelite, because it looks like a discount in exchange for future gifts. This incident tests that rule against a sale at fair market value.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A guest at Rav Ashi's home who questions the firstborn meat served to him.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The host of the visit.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage whose rule Mar Zutra cites.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Gives the reason behind the mishna Mar Zutra quotes.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat is holy and belongs to a priest. Unblemished, it is offered on the altar; an ordinary Israelite may eat one only if it has a blemish.

terms.term: a priest who assists at the threshing floor
terms.meaning: A priest who helps a farmer at harvest so the farmer will give him his priestly gifts. The Sages forbade anything that looks like trading favors for those gifts.

09.note: Rav Aḥa of Huzal had taken a vow forbidding himself any benefit from his wife, and came to Rav Ashi to have it dissolved. Rav Ashi told him to go and come back tomorrow, because he had drunk wine, and pointed out that Rav would not give public lectures on a Festival day because of drunkenness. Rav Aḥa objected that Rav ruled like Rabbi Elazar, and Rav Ashi mixed water into his wine. Rav Ashi answered that Rabbi Elazar's ruling covers a quarter-log of wine, and he had drunk more than that.
09.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Elazar, who exempts a priest who drank diluted wine. This incident tests how far that ruling reaches for a Sage asked to rule after drinking; the discussion then lists what may not be taught after wine.

people.name: Rav Aḥa of Huzal
people.about: Has vowed not to benefit from his wife and asks Rav Ashi to release him.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Puts off ruling until the next day because he has drunk wine.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Would not lecture publicly on Festival days because of drinking; ruled like Rabbi Elazar.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view on diluted wine Rav follows.

terms.meaning: A Sage can release a person from a vow he regrets; doing so counts as giving a legal ruling.
A speaker who repeated a Sage's lecture aloud to a large audience.
A small liquid measure, about a cupful; it is the amount of wine at issue in these rulings.

10.note: The Temple courtyard cried out four times: to remove Ḥofni and Pineḥas, sons of Eli, for making the Sanctuary impure; to open for Yoḥanan ben Nedavai, who ate so much that no sacrificial meat was ever left over; to let Elishama ben Pikai in as High Priest; and to expel Yissakhar from the village of Barkai, who wrapped his hands in silk to do the service. King Yannai and the queen asked this High Priest whether goat or lamb was better. He said that if goat were better it would be the daily offering, gesturing with his hand. The king ordered his right hand cut off; he bribed the official and lost his left, and the king had the right cut off too. Rav Yosef blessed God for this retribution.
10.why: The mishna teaches that although lambs are usually listed before goats in the Torah, the two are equal. Right after the story, Rav Ashi and Ravina say Yissakhar's answer shows he had not learned this mishna, or even read the Torah's verses.

people.name: Ḥofni and Pineḥas
people.about: The sons of Eli the priest, whom the courtyard demands be removed for making the Sanctuary impure.

people.name: Yoḥanan ben Nedavai
people.about: Student of Pinkai, praised for eating offerings so that no sacrificial meat was ever left over.

people.name: Elishama ben Pikai
people.about: Student of Pineḥas, whom the courtyard calls in to serve as High Priest.

people.name: Yissakhar from the village of Barkai
people.about: A High Priest who wrapped his hands in silk to avoid dirtying them in the service.

people.name: Yannai the king
people.about: Asks Yissakhar's opinion and orders his hands cut off.

terms.meaning: A large dry measure; four se'a of birds is an enormous amount.
The lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon.

11.note: Rabbi Shimon recalled that in the village of Pani an old man asked him whether Rabbi Akiva really held that sprinkling the blood takes effect even for sacrificial meat that had left the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Shimon said yes. When he reported this to his colleagues in Galilee, they asked how sprinkling could count for meat that was already unfit. He then put the matter to Rabbi Akiva, who said, my son, do you not hold so yourself, and began to argue from the case of a sin offering that was lost, replaced, and then found. The rest of his argument is not given here.
11.why: The Gemara has been examining Rabbi Akiva's view that sprinkling the blood frees meat that left the courtyard from the laws of misuse, and Rabbi Elazar's limit on it. Rabbi Shimon's account is the source of Rabbi Akiva's comparison to the lost and found sin offering.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's student, who carries a question about his teacher's view from Pani to Galilee and back to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Defends his ruling to Rabbi Shimon by comparing it to a lost and replaced sin offering.

terms.meaning: Throwing an offering's blood on the altar, the act that completes the sacrifice and permits its meat.
The offense of using consecrated Temple property for personal benefit.
An animal sacrifice brought to atone for an unintentional sin.

11.flag: Ends mid-argument: Rabbi Akiva's reply continues into the AFTER segments (Meilah 7b), so the conclusion of the exchange is cut off.

12.note: In Rome, Rabbi Matya ben Ḥarash asked Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai how we know creeping animals' blood is impure, and got a verse. He told his admiring students it was Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's tradition, and told why: Rome had forbidden Shabbat and circumcision. Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobeli, passing as a gentile, talked them out of each decree, but once they saw he was a Jew they restored them. The Sages sent Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai with Rabbi Elazar. On the road Rabbi Elazar whispered that verse in his teacher's presence, and Rabbi Shimon cursed him never to return to his father. The demon ben Temalyon possessed the emperor's daughter; Rabbi Shimon drove it out, and in the emperor's treasury they found the decree and tore it up.
12.why: The Gemara has been discussing when blood joins with flesh to make up a measure for impurity. The story is attached because it records where the teaching that creeping animals' blood is impure comes from.

people.name: Rabbi Matya ben Ḥarash
people.about: Asks Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai a question in Rome and tells the story behind the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: Sent to Rome because he is used to miracles; he drives the demon from the emperor's daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Goes with Rabbi Shimon, answers a question in his presence, and is cursed by him.

people.name: Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobeli
people.about: Disguises himself as a gentile and talks the Romans out of their decrees for a time.

people.name: ben Temalyon
people.about: A demon who offers to help and possesses the emperor's daughter.

terms.meaning: Small creatures such as rodents and lizards; the Torah declares their carcasses ritually impure.
A haircut worn only by gentiles, which let Rabbi Reuven pass as one of them.

13.note: Rav Safra was in a bathroom when Rabbi Abba came by and coughed to ask whether he might come in. Rav Safra told him: Enter, Master. When Rav Safra came out, Rabbi Abba rebuked him: you have never been to Seir, yet you have learned the ways of Seir. Did the mishna not teach that a closed door shows someone is inside, meaning that no one should go in while another person is there?
13.why: The mishna describes a dignified bathroom in the Temple whose closed door showed it was in use. The Gemara then defends Rav Safra: he feared Rabbi Abba's health would be at risk if he had to hold back.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Invites Rabbi Abba into the bathroom while he is inside.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Enters at Rav Safra's invitation and then rebukes him for it.

terms.meaning: The land of the Edomites; here a byword for people who behave immodestly.

14.note: A man drank water and, without pouring some out first, handed the cup to his student. The student was a fastidious person and would not drink from it, and he died of thirst. At that time the Sages ruled that a person should not drink water and give the rest to his student unless he first pours some of it out.
14.why: Rav and Rav Huna have just told their sons to pour out a little water before passing the cup to a student; this baraita gives the incident behind that advice. Rav Ashi draws from it that a student who pours out water in front of his teacher is not being disrespectful.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Concludes that a student may pour out water in front of his teacher without disrespect.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

15.note: Two priests were tied as they raced up the altar ramp. One of them shoved the other, and his leg was broken. When the court saw that people were coming into danger, they ruled that the ashes would be removed from the altar only by lottery.
15.why: The Gemara is reconciling two clauses of the mishna: in one, the first priest ready removes the ashes; in the other, a lottery decides. Abaye says the first describes practice before the lottery was enacted, and this incident is why it was enacted.

terms.meaning: The first Temple task each morning, clearing ashes from the altar; priests competed for the honor.
The sloping walkway priests climbed to reach the top of the altar.

16.note: Alexander of Macedon put ten questions to the Elders of the Negev: whether heaven to earth or east to west is farther, whether heaven or earth was created first, whether light or darkness came first, who is wise, mighty and rich, how a man lives and dies, how to win people's favor, and whether to live at sea or on land. They answered all but the question on light and darkness. When he called their united stand opposition and threatened to kill them, they told him falsehood does not suit a king, and he dressed them in purple with gold chains. He set out for Africa, crossed the Mountains of Darkness on their advice, and reached a town of women, who brought him bread of gold on a golden table. How that meeting ends is not given here.
16.why: The Gemara has just explained that the daily offering was slaughtered facing the sun. It brings Alexander's questions because his first one concerns the sun's place in the sky.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: A king who questions the Elders of the Negev and then sets out to conquer Africa.

people.name: the Elders of the Negev
people.about: The Sages Alexander questions, who answer him and advise him on his journey.

terms.meaning: A mountain range the Elders say blocks the way to Africa, which can be crossed only with animals that walk in the dark.
Here, the force that leads people to do what is plainly wrong; the Elders say even it sometimes wins.

16.flag: Breaks off mid-scene: the women's reply about the golden bread and Alexander's lesson fall in the AFTER segment (they open story AB7901).

17.note: Alexander asked the women whether people eat bread of gold. They replied that if he only wanted bread, he had bread at home; that was not why he had come. On leaving, he wrote on the town gate: I, Alexander of Macedon, was a fool until I came to the land of Africa of women, and I learned sense from women. Later, eating salted fish by a spring, he smelled a fragrance and concluded the spring came from the Garden of Eden. Some say he followed it to Eden's gate and demanded entry; refused, he asked for something, and was given an eyeball that outweighed all his gold and silver. The Sages told him the human eye is never satisfied, and once he covered it with dirt, it balanced.
17.why: This continues the Gemara's account of Alexander, which began with his questions to the Elders of the Negev and his march to Africa. After it, the Gemara adds a teaching that Gehenna lies beyond the Mountains of Darkness he crossed.

people.name: Alexander of Macedon
people.about: A king on campaign in Africa, who learns from a town of women and seeks entry to the Garden of Eden.

terms.meaning: Paradise, the garden of the first humans; here its gate is guarded and only the righteous may enter.

18.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once ruled in a woman's case according to Rabbi Eliezer, who held that a woman who had gone three expected cycles without bleeding is impure only from the moment she sees blood, not retroactively. Afterward, when he remembered that many Sages, not just one, disagreed with Rabbi Eliezer, he said: Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in exigent circumstances.
18.why: Rav Huna holds that a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity affects only sacrificial food, not teruma. The Gemara argues that since there was no sacrificial food in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's day, this case must have involved teruma, which challenges Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Rules according to Rabbi Eliezer and then defends relying on him in a time of need.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose opinion, disputed by many colleagues, is followed in this case.

terms.meaning: A situation of pressing need or hardship, when a Sage may rely on a minority opinion.
The rule that a woman who finds menstrual blood is treated as impure for a period before she found it, so things she touched then become impure too.

19.note: Rabban Gamliel's maidservant was baking loaves of teruma, and between each loaf she washed her hand and examined herself. After the last one she found she was impure from menstrual blood, and she asked Rabban Gamliel. He told her all the loaves were impure. She said: My teacher, did I not examine myself between each one? He answered: If so, this last one is impure and all the rest are pure.
19.why: Rav Huna holds that a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity reaches sacrificial food but not teruma. Since Rabban Gamliel applied it to teruma loaves, the Gemara cites this as a challenge, then answers that these were loaves of a thanks offering.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rules on the status of the loaves his maidservant baked.

terms.meaning: The portion of produce given to priests, which must be kept ritually pure.
A woman checks for menstrual blood, since finding it makes her ritually impure and can make what she touched impure as well.

20.note: Another time, Rabban Gamliel's maidservant was sealing barrels of wine, washing her hands and examining herself between each one. After the last one she found she was impure, and she asked Rabban Gamliel, who said all the barrels were impure. She reminded him that she had examined herself between each one, and he ruled: If so, this last one is impure and all the rest are pure.
20.why: The Gemara is testing Rav Huna's view that retroactive menstrual impurity applies to sacrificial food but not teruma. If both incidents involved sacrificial food, why would she ask twice? The Gemara answers that they happened to two different maidservants.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rules on the status of the wine barrels his maidservant sealed.

terms.meaning: A woman checks for menstrual blood, since finding it makes her ritually impure and can make what she touched impure as well.
